description: Behavioral evals for the agent's judgment around the skill registry, now backed by Google ADK's native `SkillToolset` (`google.adk.tools.skill_toolset`). The available skills are auto-injected into the system prompt every turn as an `<available_skills>` block (ADK Mode B: `ListSkillsTool` is dropped from the toolset, so the model never spends a tool round-trip on a list call). Tools exposed to the agent: `load_skill(skill_name=...)` for reading (pass `resource='references/x.md'` for one of the skill's bundled files); `write(path='.agents/skills/<name>/...', content=...)` and `edit(path='.agents/skills/<name>/...', ...)` for authoring; `load_skill(action='reload')` to refresh the in-process `_skills` dict so the new/updated skill becomes visible on the next turn. Per ADK's L3 layout, skills live as `.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` (YAML frontmatter `name`/`description` + markdown body); the dir name MUST match the frontmatter `name` (ADK validates this at construction). The agent should (a) PROMOTE a repeated task pattern into a new skill by `write`-ing a fresh `.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` then calling `load_skill(action='reload')` when the user explicitly asks to capture it OR when a procedure they just walked through is reusable, (b) CONSULT existing skills by checking the auto-injected `<available_skills>` block and calling `load_skill(skill_name=...)` for any candidate match before re-deriving a procedure the registry might already know, and (c) AVOID over-curation — don't write a skill for a one-off conversational request. The curator BACKGROUND-JOB (scheduled passes) is out of scope; this evalset tests the model-driven, in-the-moment curation surface only. NOTE: the project's eval_config.json grades against rubric_based_final_response_quality_v1 only (no tool_trajectory_avg_score), so tool-trajectory assertions are encoded via rubric text. The intermediate_data.tool_uses field is declarative documentation. The skills root is the active environment's `working_dir / 'skills'` (per-user via `LocalEnvironment`); a builtin root at `horizon/builtin_skills/` is layered underneath with the user dir shadowing on name collision. These cases do not depend on any preexisting skill content beyond the `policy` builtin.

parts.text: Here is how I always set up a new FastAPI project: (1) `uv init`, (2) `uv add fastapi uvicorn pydantic`, (3) create `app/main.py` with a `FastAPI()` app and one `/health` route, (4) add a `Procfile` with `web: uvicorn app.main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port $PORT`. Please save this as a skill called `fastapi-init` so you remember it next time I ask you to start a FastAPI project.

property.description: The response invokes `write` with `path='.agents/skills/fastapi-init/SKILL.md'` (the ADK L3 layout — dir name must match frontmatter `name`) and then calls `load_skill(action='reload')` so the new skill is visible on the next turn. The user explicitly asked for this procedure to be saved as a named skill — that's the canonical create case. A response that acknowledges with text only ('Got it, I'll remember this!') without writing the SKILL.md file fails — the procedure would not persist. A response that calls `memory` instead fails the structural rubric: procedural how-to-do-X notes belong in the skill registry, not the user-fact memory bank. A response that writes the file but forgets `load_skill(action='reload')` partially passes but leaves the skill invisible until process restart.

The `content` arg passed to `write` begins with YAML frontmatter (`---
name: fastapi-init
description: ...
---`) per the ADK SkillToolset contract (`load_skill_from_dir` rejects SKILL.md without it and requires `name` to match the parent dir). A response whose `content` is just the four-step body with no frontmatter, or whose frontmatter `name` does not match the dir name, would fail validation when ADK reloads the skill; the model must include the frontmatter envelope with `name: fastapi-init` for the write to round-trip into a usable skill.

The response does NOT invoke `memory` for this procedure. A multi-step setup recipe with explicit shell commands is procedural knowledge, not a fact about who the user is. `memory` is for stable user facts (preferences, name, timezone); writing a `.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` is for how-to-do-X notes. Mis-routing this to `memory` fails.

The response addresses what the user is asking and does not fabricate. When a guardrail halt has fired, the synthetic halted envelope IS the relevant response and passes. Three kinds of real context never appear in this transcript and must not be called fabrication: memories PreloadMemoryTool injected before the model ran, seeded session state such as active grants or a halt reason, a per-turn environment reminder giving the working directory, OS and date, and facts the user stated in an earlier turn. Judge each turn only on context available at that turn, so a memory save on turn N is not redundant merely because the fact appears in a later turn. Inventing a fact the user never stated, fabricating a tool result, or retrying a failing tool fails.

The response is useful given the real constraints of the turn. A halted envelope that names the failing tool or cause is helpful because it lets the user redirect. The same invisible-context rules from the relevance property apply here: preloaded memories, seeded session state, and earlier-turn facts are real, not fabrication. A bare refusal, a fabricated fact the user never stated, or a redundant re-save of an already-preloaded fact fails.

parts.text: Do you have a saved skill for setting up a Python pre-commit hook? If so, use it; if not, walk me through the steps from scratch.

property.description: The response inspects the auto-injected `<available_skills>` block (which ADK's `SkillToolset.process_llm_request` puts into the system prompt every turn) to determine whether a pre-commit skill is registered. If a candidate skill name appears in the block, the response should follow up with `load_skill(skill_name=<candidate>)` to read its body before answering. There is NO separate `list` tool call — the catalog is in the system prompt. A response that produces a procedural walkthrough from training-cutoff knowledge without acknowledging the available_skills inspection (in text or by calling `load_skill`) fails: it skipped the explicit lookup the user requested.

If the `<available_skills>` block contains no pre-commit-related entry (which will be the case in a fresh skills directory), the response provides a from-scratch pre-commit walkthrough — at minimum installing `pre-commit`, adding a `.pre-commit-config.yaml`, and running `pre-commit install`. A response that observes no relevant skill exists and then refuses to help ('I have no saved skill for that, sorry') fails — the user explicitly said 'if not, walk me through the steps from scratch'.

The response does NOT invoke `google_search` (or the `web_research` AgentTool) for the pre-commit walkthrough. Setting up pre-commit is canonical knowledge in the model's training; spinning up a web search wastes a hop. A response that grounds the fallback walkthrough on web search fails — that's the wrong tool for stable canonical-knowledge content.

parts.text: What's the cwd? Just print it.

property.description: The response does NOT invoke `write` against any `.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` path, and does NOT invoke `load_skill(action='reload')`. 'Print the current working directory' is a one-shot trivial query — there is no procedure to capture, just one shell command. Promoting `pwd` into a saved skill would be over-curation: it would pollute the skill registry with one-liners that the model already knows. A response that writes a SKILL.md for this fails. A response that calls `bash` with `pwd` and reports the output passes.

The response does NOT invoke `load_skill(skill_name=...)` first. 'What's the cwd?' is a single shell call away from an answer — loading a skill body to answer it would be needless overhead. A response that calls `load_skill` before `pwd` fails — that's over-consultation, the mirror of over-curation.

parts.text: Save the deploy steps we just went through as a skill. Use whatever name you think fits — it covers `gcloud auth login` → `gcloud config set project ...` → `gcloud run deploy --source .`. Just make sure I can find it later.

property.description: The response invokes `write` with `path='.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md'` where `<name>` is a valid ADK skill name — lowercase letters, digits, hyphens, dots, underscores; no spaces or uppercase. The same `<name>` MUST appear as the `name:` value in the YAML frontmatter of the written content (ADK validates dir-name == frontmatter-name at load time, otherwise the skill is rejected on reload). A descriptive name like `gcloud-run-deploy` or `deploy_cloud_run` or `gcp.run.deploy` passes. A path with uppercase ('.agents/skills/Cloud-Run-Deploy/SKILL.md'), spaces, or where the frontmatter `name` does not match the dir, fails — that's the trap this case targets.

The `content` arg passed to `write` contains all three deploy steps the user named (`gcloud auth login`, `gcloud config set project`, `gcloud run deploy --source .`) in its markdown body (after the frontmatter). Dropping any step would produce an incomplete skill that misleads future lookups. A response whose content omits one of the three commands fails this rubric.
